summary: The note describes Old English as a West Germanic language that developed from North Sea Germanic dialects brought by the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, and that replaced Common Brittonic and Latin as Anglo-Saxon power grew. It covers the four main dialects (Mercian, Northumbrian, Kentish, West Saxon), their geographic areas, and the spread of Old English across England and parts of Scotland. It also notes Celtic and Norse survivals and how West Saxon became the standard after Viking conquests and Alfred the Great's consolidation.
one_line: Overview of Old English, the West Germanic language of Anglo-Saxon England, its four dialects, and the rise of West Saxon as standard.
key_facts: Old English developed from Anglo-Frisian or North Sea Germanic dialects spoken by the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes.
Old English replaced Common Brittonic, a Celtic language, and Latin, which had been brought to Britain by the Roman invasion.
Old English had four main dialects: Mercian, Northumbrian, Kentish and West Saxon.
Mercian and Northumbrian are together referred to as Anglian.
The Northumbrian region lay north of the Humber River, while the Mercian region lay north of the Thames and south of the Humber River.
West Saxon lay south and southwest of the Thames, and Kentish lay southeast of the Thames.
The Kentish region, settled by the Jutes from Jutland, has the scantiest literary remains.
West Saxon formed the basis for the literary standard of the later Old English period, while Middle and Modern English mainly developed from Mercian.
Scandinavian rule and settlement beginning in the 9th century brought strong Old Norse influence to eastern and northern England.
Old English developed out of Ingvaeonic (North Sea Germanic) dialects from the 5th century.
Medieval Cornish was spoken all over Cornwall and in adjacent parts of Devon.
Cumbric survived perhaps to the 12th century in parts of Cumbria.
Northumbria south of the Tyne, and most of Mercia, were overrun by the Vikings during the 9th century.
The portion of Mercia that was successfully defended, and all of Kent, were integrated into Wessex under Alfred the Great.
After Alfred the Great's consolidation, the Early West Saxon dialect became standardised as the language of government and of literature and religious works.
